41227-gairloch-in-north-west-ross-shire-:
John Dixon's account of Gairloch, a Highland parish in north-west Ross-shire, was printed at Edinburgh in 1886, with chapters by William Jolly, John McMurtrie, and Ivison Macadam. The book joins the parish's records, traditions, and inhabitants to its natural history, and adds a guide to Gairloch and Loch Maree with a map. It is dedicated to Sir Kenneth Mackenzie, sixth baronet and thirteenth laird of Gairloch.

Dixon writes from regard, almost affection, for the parish, hoping to help the tourist and to earn a nook in the library of local history. Sir Kenneth and Lady Mackenzie gave information and help freely, as did Osgood Mackenzie of Inverewe. Alexander Mackenzie's history of the Mackenzies and his Celtic Magazine supplied much of the clan matter.
45075-life-and-adventures-of-billy-dixon:
Life and Adventures of Billy Dixon is the memoir of a Texas Panhandle scout and buffalo hunter. Bat Masterson praised Dixon in its pages. The fight at Adobe Walls and the Buffalo Wallow engagement, for which Congress voted the Medal of Honor, are its climaxes.

The narrative begins in West Virginia and Missouri. Orphaned, Dixon ran away to the plains, became a bull-whacker out of Leavenworth, and killed his first buffalo as a boy. By eighteen he was hunting hides, running a road ranch, and scouting in country the chapter headings call dangerous. Dodge City in 1872, the Cimarron, prowl­ing Cheyennes and the founding of Adobe Walls fill the middle chapters. It is a dictated frontier life, plain and boastful in the plains manner.
54613-the-battle-for-khe-sanh:
The Battle for Khe Sanh is the official Marine Corps monograph on the siege. Captain Moyers Shore wrote it for the History and Museums Division at Headquarters, and it was printed in 1969, while the Vietnam War still ran. An oblique aerial photograph of the combat base fronts the text.

Khe Sanh was a hill base near the Laotian border. North Vietnamese divisions besieged it for over two months in early 1968, and American airpower and artillery held it at enormous cost. Official histories of this series record operations in staff detail: units, dates, tonnages, and lessons drawn while the war continued. The monograph is both a record and an argument, the Corps explaining to itself what the siege had meant and what it had cost.
6607-myths-and-legends-of-our-own-land-v:
Dolph Heyliger, a graceless but brave New York lad, opens the second volume, set on the Isle of Manhattoes and nearby shores. Left poor when his father dies, Dolph takes service with a doctor who owns a farm out where Twenty-third Street now runs. Rumors about the place, and tenants who whisper of it, soon pull him into trouble.

Other tales in the volume follow: a knell at a wedding, roistering Dutchmen, a party from Gibbet Island, and the devil's stepping-stones. Skinner keeps the old New Amsterdam flavor, with Dutch names and harbor lore. This volume is a charming, ghostly tour of early New York and its near waters.
67468-smuggling-smugglers-in-sussex-the-:
Smuggling and Smugglers in Sussex gives the history of the murders of William Galley, a custom-house officer, and Daniel Chater, a shoemaker, by a gang of fourteen smugglers. The account was first published in 1749, soon after seven of the men were tried and hanged at Chichester.

The writer says he took the facts from the mouths of witnesses and talked with the prisoners before and after their sentencing. Seven plates show the cruelty of the killings. Added trials cover John Mills and Henry Sheerman, and Thomas Kingsmill and others who broke open the custom house at Poole. The volume also holds a sermon preached at the special assize and a later paper on smuggling in Sussex.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-AtzenhofferAnth:
On January 24, 1964, FBI agents in Dallas interviewed Anthony 'Tony' Atzenhoffer Jr. as part of the Kennedy assassination investigation. Atzenhoffer had been a cadet in the Civil Air Patrol, and the Bureau wanted his memory of a fellow cadet from years before: Lee Harvey Oswald.

The interview report records his recollection that Oswald had been in the Civil Air Patrol in New Orleans. The cadet squadron there was once commanded by David Ferrie, a figure who later drew investigators' attention. Single interview reports like this one are the bricks of the FBI's Oswald file, each testing one small claim against a witness.
myths-and-legends-of-our-own-land-volume:
Charles M. Skinner devotes this volume to Manhattan and lands nearby. Dolph Heyliger opens the tales in old New Amsterdam. Dolph was a brave, penniless scamp left by his father's death. He took service with a doctor who owned a haunted farm.

Rumors kept tenants off that farm, up where Twenty-third Street now runs. Dolph was sent to spend three nights in the lone manor. He came out pale but kept his counsel, to the town's rage. Wedding knells, devil's stepping-stones, and bloody springs fill the contents. Skinner finds thick folklore under the modern city's streets and farms.
